parts:

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: How to boost analysis performance
parts:
Hi Edu,

The R interpreter is single-threaded, so unfortunately it can be difficult to take advantage of multiple cores or processors in R. Code must be written specifically for it, and Cardinal is not currently written to take advantage of the parallel package in R. Because the R interpreter is single-threaded, the parallel package works by spawning additional R processes, each of which have their own memory footprint. Necessary objects are copied over, so it can be very memory-inefficient for large datasets. We are still thinking about the best way to take advantage of multiple cores/processors in Cardinal.

-Kyle

messages.author: 6033d3c0e7d242fa
messages.subject: Re: How to boost analysis performance
parts:
It's possible. In the future, it will probably be an option, using the 'foreach' and 'doParallel' packages. Indeed, I designed it that way to make it easier to add in the future. However, the problem remains for the time being that most of these packages currently rely on spawning additional R processes and duplicating objects in memory, making them very memory-inefficient for large datasets. It is possible to use shared memory approaches such as the 'bigmemory' package to get around this, but at the time of writing Cardinal, I didn't want to make this a requirement, since it was broken on Windows at the time (it seems to be fixed now). It will be coming eventually, but I want to figure out how to do it in a way that imposes the least unexpected problems (e.g., memory inefficiency) and fewest additional requirements on users.

-K

messages.author: 23c079b0573006a3
messages.subject: Re: How to boost analysis performance
parts:
I wrote a parallel function using snow for ReduceDimension, where I did ReduceDimension over 50+ imzmls using a previously generated common peaklist, but like Kyle said, it requires loading the cardinal package, imzml file and peaklist into each instance of R, which was fine as the datasets were not large and I have 64 GB RAM..here's the function I wrote, it can give others some ideas, basically it sped up the peak processing by 8x using all 8 threads, but gets close to filling all the RAM. I wrote it a long time ago (when I was less advanced) so its probably not very efficient..


##mywd = directory where the imzmls files are kept
##no_clus = number of clusters to run parallel, should be <= total
##peaklist = previously generated cardinal peaklist or vector of mz values

ReduceDimensionParallel <- function(peaklist, mywd_=getwd(),no_clus=4){
  
  imzmllist <- gsub(".imzML","",list.files(path=mywd,pattern="*.imzML"))
  imzmllist <- as.list(c(imzmllist))
  ppeaklist <- peaklist
  
  require(snow)
  
  cl <- makeCluster(no_clus)
  clusterEvalQ(cl, library(Cardinal)) 
  clusterExport(cl, "imzmllist") 
  clusterExport(cl, "ppeaklist")
  
  peakdata <- parLapply(cl, imzmllist, function(x){
    rawd <-readImzML(x,folder=mywd)
    rawd <-normalize(rawd, method=c("tic"))
    peakd <- reduceDimension(rawd, ref = ppeaklist, type = "height")
    rm(rawd)
    gc()
    return(peakd)
  })
  
  stopCluster(cl)
  return(peakdata)}

messages.subject: Re: How to boost analysis performance
parts:
Hi Denis,

Parallel computing in R is enough of its own topic that general tips is a bit beyond the scope of what I can help you with right now.

I would suggest try running some simple examples from the 'parallel' package before trying to do something more complicated. Here are some places to get started:

https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/parallel/doc/parallel.pdf
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/doParallel/vignettes/gettingstartedParallel.pdf
http://www.r-bloggers.com/how-to-go-parallel-in-r-basics-tips/

You have some options to choose from in the 'parallel' package with the par *apply functions, or the 'foreach' approach.

If you're not worried about compatibility and portability (since you're writing code for yourself), then it may be simpler to stick to the 'parallel' package.

I find the 'mclapply' from the 'parallel' package is the easiest and most straightforward since it forks the whole R session and you don't have to worry about managing which objects are copied. However, it only works on *nix operating systems, so on Windows you're limited to the SNOW approach.

I'm sorry I can't be more help right now. I hope to have better support for larger datasets and parallel options later this year.

-Ky
